To waddle means to walk by swaying your body from side to side, taking short steps, shifting your weight left and right with every step you take. Instead of moving smoothly forward, a waddling creature rocks like a boat — left, right, left, right — with each step.
What does it actually look like?

Picture a duck walking. Its body is wide and low, its legs are short and set far apart, and its feet point outward. When it walks, it can't help but tilt its whole body to one side with each step, then tilt to the other side for the next step. It moves forward, yes — but it looks clumsy and rocking. That rocking, side-to-side, short-stepped walk is a waddle.

A penguin is another perfect example. It stands upright but has a chubby round body and tiny short legs. When it walks, it swings from side to side like a living pendulum. It almost looks like it might tip over, but it doesn't. That is waddling.

Waddling happens because of a physical condition that makes smooth, straight walking difficult or impossible. The causes include:

  • A wide or heavy body — When someone's legs are set far apart due to a wide body or extra weight, they have to tilt to shift their weight over each foot. Overweight people sometimes waddle for this reason.
  • A round belly — A pregnant woman in her final months often develops a waddle because her large belly shifts her center of gravity forward and forces her hips to swing out with each step.
  • Short legs relative to body size — This is why ducks and penguins waddle. Their legs are simply too short and too far apart to allow a straight walk.
  • Injury or pain — Someone with a hip or knee problem may waddle to avoid putting full pressure on the painful side.

The key point: waddling is not a choice. It is caused by the body's shape, weight, or condition.

Normal walking keeps the body mostly upright and stable. The head and torso move relatively straight ahead. In waddling, the whole upper body visibly sways side to side. It is slower, more effortful, and looks awkward or clumsy compared to a regular walk. The steps are also shorter than normal.
How to use it in a sentence

The verb is used very naturally with a direction or destination:

  • "The duck waddled toward the pond."
  • "The penguin waddled across the ice."
  • "She waddled into the room, eight months pregnant."
  • "He ate so much at dinner that he waddled back to his car."
  • "A group of ducklings waddled behind their mother in a line."

You can also use it without a destination:

  • "Look at how that penguin waddles!"
  • "The baby, still learning to walk, waddled and nearly fell."
The tone and feeling of the word

Waddle carries a slightly humorous, affectionate, or comic quality. When you say an animal waddles, it sounds cute and funny — nobody is being insulted. When you say a person waddles, it describes their gait honestly, but it does carry a mild sense of clumsiness or awkwardness. It is not a harsh insult, but it is not entirely neutral either — it suggests the walk looks a little funny. In casual speech, it can even be used in a warm, teasing, or playful way.

The word can also be used as a noun,. Just so you are aware: "She walked with a waddle" means her way of walking was a waddling gait. "The penguin's waddle was adorable" describes the characteristic way it moves. The noun form describes the same physical motion — it is just used as a thing rather than an action.
A one-line summary to remember it forever
To waddle = to walk with a rocking, side-to-side sway and short steps, the way a duck or penguin moves.
